stories.headline: Iran war flares again: Hormuz mine claims, drones at Bahrain
stories.question: Why has the Iran war suddenly flared again, with mines in Hormuz and a strike on Bahrain?
stories.dek: Neither side has let go. The US still blockades Iran's ports, and Iran polices Hormuz. Now Iran claims mine hits and a drone strike, while the Houthis press Saudi oil's bypass route.

so_far.text: The war that began on 28 February 2026 never fully stopped. The US still keeps a naval blockade on Iranian ports. Iran restricts which ships may pass the Strait of Hormuz and attacks ships it says break its rules. In Yemen, the Iran-backed Houthis have escalated since September. Reuters sources say Trump may hold off new attacks unless Tehran or the Houthis provoke him.

what_happened.text: On 14 November Iran's navy said three oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Its Revolutionary Guards said the ships tried a prohibited route. Reuters could not verify this, and nobody has said who laid the mines. On 15 November Reuters reported the Guards attacked a US base in Bahrain with six drones, calling it retaliation for 'hostile US actions'. The US military said it intercepted two drones, with no damage. Bahrain said it intercepted several attacks, its first since September. In Yemen, Saudi-backed government forces pulled back from Bab el-Mandeb to defend Aden, while the Houthis claimed strikes on Riyadh and a Saudi oil pipeline.

steps.text: The US keeps a naval blockade on Iranian ports, squeezing Iran's trade even without new strikes.
Iran keeps its own grip: it restricts which ships may pass Hormuz and attacks those it says break its rules.
The Revolutionary Guards called the Bahrain drone attack retaliation for 'hostile US actions'; the sources do not say which actions.
In Yemen, government forces retreated, and the Houthis claim hits on the pipeline Saudi Arabia uses to bypass Hormuz.
The unpopular war hurt Republicans in the midterms; Reuters sources say Trump may hold off strikes unless provoked.

history.text: It starts in 1979, when the Islamic Revolution overthrew the Shah and Iran cut ties with the US. In 2015 Iran signed the JCPOA nuclear deal. In 2018 Trump withdrew the US and reimposed sanctions under a policy called 'maximum pressure'. In 2020 the US killed Qasem Soleimani. In June 2025 the 'Twelve-Day War' saw Israel and the US strike Iranian nuclear and military sites, followed by a ceasefire. UN 'snapback' sanctions, which bring back earlier UN penalties, returned in September 2025. On 28 February 2026 the US and Israel struck again, killing Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Iran blocked Hormuz and attacked Israel, US bases and Gulf states. From then on, shipping became the main battlefield. A ceasefire began on 8 April, but Iran resumed its Hormuz closure. After talks in Islamabad failed on 12–13 April, the US imposed a naval blockade on Iran. Now each side gripped the other's shipping. A 17 June memorandum lifted this 'dual blockade', but the ceasefire collapsed on 8 July after Iran attacked commercial ships in Hormuz. From September the Iran-backed Houthis escalated Yemen's civil war, opening a second chokepoint crisis at Bab el-Mandeb. In October they attacked Saudi airports.

lesson.concept: How Gulf oil gets out when Hormuz is squeezed
lesson.big_idea: Gulf oil reaches the world through a front door, the Strait of Hormuz, and a few back doors, like pipelines to the Red Sea. Supply is whatever gets through all the doors combined.

steps.title: Gulf oil leaves by sea
steps.text: Most oil from the Persian Gulf is carried away by tankers. The only sea exit from the Gulf is the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow channel. Think of it as the front door.

steps.title: Squeezing the front door
steps.text: You don't need to stop every ship. Route rules, attacks on rule-breakers or reports of mines make shipowners slow down or stay away. Iran restricts ships in Hormuz and says three tankers hit mines.

steps.title: Pipelines are back doors
steps.text: A pipeline can carry oil overland to a port outside the Gulf. Saudi Arabia has rerouted about 4 million barrels a day through its East-West pipeline to Yanbu, on the Red Sea.

steps.title: Back doors have weak spots
steps.text: Pumping stations push oil along a pipeline; damage them and flow can fall. Tankers leaving Yanbu southward must also pass Bab el-Mandeb, where Yemen's war is spreading.

steps.title: Supply is the sum
steps.text: Oil reaching buyers equals what passes the front door plus what the back doors carry. Squeeze both at once and the losses add up.

example.setup: Say a Gulf country normally exports 10 million barrels of oil a day, all by tanker through Hormuz. It also has a pipeline to the Red Sea. All numbers here are assumed.

lines.note: All of it normally passes Hormuz.

example.result: Squeezing one door costs supply; squeezing both makes the losses stack. Here the country loses 4.5 million of its 10 million barrels a day, nearly half.

apply.text: That is why recent days look like one squeeze from several sides. Iran restricts the front door, Hormuz, and says three tankers hit mines. The Houthis claim they hit two pumping stations on the pipeline carrying about 4 million barrels a day to Yanbu, though Saudi Arabia did not confirm. And government forces have pulled back from the Bab el-Mandeb area.

practice.q: Same country: Hormuz still lets 3 million through and the pipeline works fully at 5 million, but Red Sea risks stop 1 million of pipeline oil sailing. What reaches buyers?
practice.answer: Pipeline oil that sails: 5 − 1 = 4 million. Add Hormuz: 3 + 4 = 7 million. Shortfall: 10 − 7 = 3 million barrels a day. The back door's own exit matters too.

stories.headline: Manila defence pact and Quad talks open Asia's summit week
stories.question: What is at stake for India and China in Asia's week of back-to-back summits?
stories.dek: Australia and the Philippines tightened military ties on 15 November. Quad leaders, including India's, may meet on 17 November. China hosts APEC and a planned Trump–Xi–Putin meeting on 19 November.

so_far.text: Several summits are packed into one week. The ASEAN summit, a yearly meeting of Southeast Asian leaders, opened in Manila on 15 November and runs three days. Leaders will discuss the Middle East war, Myanmar and South China Sea disputes. The Philippines then hands ASEAN's chair to Singapore. APEC, a Pacific-rim trade forum, gathers in Shenzhen, China, from 17 November. The US–China agenda there covers trade, chip exports and rare-earth controls. On 19 November, Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin plan their first-ever three-way meeting. US officials expect no concrete deal. Beijing had not publicly confirmed it.

what_happened.text: On 15 November in Manila, Australia and the Philippines signed a new defence cooperation pact. It aims at deeper military ties as both face a more assertive China. Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro said it puts their existing Status of Forces Agreement into practice. That means no more multiple permits, quicker joint training and faster Australian disaster response. The pact also expands maritime surveillance and information sharing. The report on his remarks lists no binding duty to defend each other. Separately, Quad leaders from the US, Japan, Australia and India are expected to meet in Manila on 17 November. That meeting is not officially confirmed.

steps.text: Australia and the Philippines both face a more assertive China, and in August 2026 condemned its actions against Philippine vessels.
Help is slow if every joint exercise or relief mission needs several separate permits.
The new pact cuts that paperwork, so Australian forces can train, watch the sea and respond faster.
China has called Philippine drills with Australia courting outside powers, yet the same week it hosts APEC and talks trade with Trump.
For India, a Quad meeting would show the grouping still works after a two-year gap.

history.text: The Australia–Philippines link goes back to 1995, when the two countries signed a defence cooperation memorandum. An unverified summary says the new pact updates and replaces it. The Quad is the second thread. Its leaders last met in Delaware in September 2024, before Trump returned to office. In May 2026, Asia Times described the grouping as 'on life support'. It pointed to a testy Trump–Modi call and a cancelled Trump trip to India. The sea is the third thread. In August 2025, after Philippine drills with Australia, a Chinese defence spokesperson said the Philippines 'has repeatedly courted influence from outside powers to make waves'. That remains China's standing line. In August 2026, Australia and the Philippines condemned China's actions against Philippine vessels. They also welcomed progress on the new arrangement. On 3 November 2026, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that the next Quad leaders' summit would be in Manila. These three threads now meet in one city.

lesson.concept: The ladder of defence ties between countries
lesson.big_idea: Countries can be linked loosely or tightly. At the bottom, they talk and set goals. In the middle, they make it easier for troops to visit. At the top, they promise to fight for each other.

steps.title: Rung one: talking together
steps.text: The lightest tie is a grouping where leaders meet and agree shared goals. The Quad's expected agenda in Manila is critical minerals, shipping lanes and attacks on commercial ships.

steps.title: Rung two: rules for visiting troops
steps.text: A Status of Forces Agreement sets the legal rules when one country's troops are on another's soil: who may enter, and under what law. The Philippines and Australia already have one.

steps.title: Rung three: making it practical
steps.text: A cooperation arrangement puts those rules to work. It swaps case-by-case permits for standing procedures, so exercises, sea surveillance and disaster help start faster. The 15 November pact is this kind.

steps.title: Rung four: a promise to fight
steps.text: The top rung is a mutual-defence treaty: an attack on one counts as an attack on both. Reports on the new pact list no such binding duty.

steps.title: Why rivals still react
steps.text: Ties below the top rung can still draw a reaction. After Philippine drills with Australia in August 2025, China's defence spokesperson said Manila courts outside powers 'to make waves'.

example.setup: Imagine Australia wants to send a navy ship to help the Philippines after a typhoon. Assume each permit takes one week to get.

example.result: The pact changes speed, not obligation. In our made-up case, help arrives two weeks sooner, but neither country has promised to go to war for the other.

apply.text: So the 15 November pact sits on rung three: it makes Australian help faster, but reports list no promise to fight. A Quad meeting on 17 November would sit on rung one for India: leaders talking about minerals and shipping lanes. China's official reaction to the new pact is not yet known.

practice.q: Suppose a joint drill needs 4 separate permits, each taking 2 weeks, and the pact replaces them with one 2-week clearance. How much time is saved?
practice.answer: Old way: 4 permits × 2 weeks = 8 weeks. New way: one clearance = 2 weeks. Saved: 8 − 2 = 6 weeks. The drill starts six weeks sooner, but nobody has promised to fight for anyone.

scenes.say: Chaliye ek example dekhte hain. Maan lijiye typhoon ke baad Australia ek navy ship bhejta hai. Aur har permit mein ek hafta lagta hai. Purana tareeka: 3 permits, 3 hafte. Naya tareeka: ek clearance, ek hafta. 2 hafte bach gaye. Lekin ladne ki duty kahin nahi dikhti.

stories.headline: Zelensky says US raised Donbas-for-NATO; Estonia to close Russia border
stories.question: Is the US asking Ukraine to swap Donbas for NATO, as Europe braces for sabotage?
stories.dek: Not formally. Zelensky says US negotiators asked whether Ukraine would leave Donbas if it joined NATO. Washington has not commented. Estonia is closing its Russian border after a foiled sabotage plot.

so_far.text: Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. US negotiators are now involved in peace talks. At talks in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 November 2026, Russia and Ukraine agreed in principle on a large prisoner exchange. No number or date was given. Big gaps remain on territory, security guarantees and NATO. Moscow rejected an energy ceasefire there. Washington wants European governments at the table, but Moscow has so far said no.

what_happened.text: On 14 November 2026 the Kyiv Independent reported that President Volodymyr Zelensky said US negotiators had asked whether Ukraine would withdraw from Donbas if it joined NATO. He said it was the first time the question had been raised. He said he cannot decide alone and wants Article 5-style guarantees as an "absolute minimum". Washington and NATO have not commented. On 15 November Estonia said it will close all three border crossings with Russia from 1 December, after a foiled arson plot that Estonian authorities say Russia's GRU ordered.

steps.text: Russia calls Ukraine joining NATO a red line, and Moscow still insists Ukraine hand over all of Donbas.
Ukraine refuses to recognise occupied land as Russian and wants strong protection against another attack.
The question Zelensky describes ties the two together: Ukraine leaves Donbas, and in return gets NATO's protection.
But that trade needs NATO allies to back it and Russia to accept a membership it calls a red line.
Separately, Estonia blames Russia's GRU for a foiled arson plot, and says closing its border will curb hostile activity and sanctions evasion.

history.text:
The story begins in 2008. At its Bucharest summit, NATO said Ukraine and Georgia would become members one day. But it offered no Membership Action Plan, the formal route to joining. Putin strongly opposed this. Ukraine got a promise without protection.

In February–March 2014, after President Yanukovych fled, Russian troops occupied Crimea. Russia annexed it after a referendum widely called illegitimate. In April 2014 Russian-backed militants seized towns in eastern Ukraine and proclaimed the Donetsk and Luhansk "People's Republics". That started the war in Donbas.

In February 2015 Russia and Ukraine signed Minsk II. It was never fully implemented, and the front line became largely static.

In February 2022 Russia recognised the two "republics" and launched a full-scale invasion. In September 2022 it declared Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia annexed. The international community condemned this.

A December 2025 report said Russia wants a deal based on Putin's 2024 conditions: Ukraine leaves Donbas, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, and renounces NATO. In that position, giving up land and giving up NATO come as one package. The question Zelensky now describes links the same two things the other way round: Ukraine leaves Donbas, but joins NATO.

lesson.concept: How NATO's Article 5 promise of defence works
lesson.big_idea: NATO members promise that an armed attack on one counts as an attack on all. The promise aims to stop wars before they start, because an attacker would face the whole alliance.

steps.title: One treaty, one promise
steps.text: Article 5 of NATO's founding treaty says an armed attack on any member is treated as an attack on every member. A small country suddenly has big friends.

steps.title: Each ally chooses how
steps.text: The treaty lets each member take the action it judges necessary, which can include armed force. It does not automatically send any one country's troops.

steps.title: Deterrence is the real point
steps.text: Deterrence means stopping an attack by making it look too costly. The promise works only if the attacker believes the allies will really act.

steps.title: Getting in needs everyone
steps.text: A new member joins only if all existing members agree. NATO promised Ukraine membership in 2008 but gave no joining plan, and Russia calls it a red line.

steps.title: "Article 5-style" means a copy
steps.text: A guarantee modelled on Article 5, given outside NATO. Zelensky calls it an absolute minimum; Washington reportedly says no US troops would be on Ukrainian soil.

example.setup: Imagine a small country with an army of 20 units. Its neighbour has 100. It joins an alliance with nine other countries, each with 30 units (assume these numbers).

lines.label: Alone
lines.note: The neighbour is five times stronger.

lines.label: Allies' strength
lines.note: What the alliance promise adds.

lines.label: Together
lines.note: The attacker now faces 290, not 20.

lines.label: Ratio flipped
lines.note: Defenders are now almost three times stronger.

lines.label: Attacker's choice
lines.calc: Attack looks too costly, so no war
lines.note: That is deterrence: the promise prevents the fight.

example.result: The promise turns a weak country into part of a much stronger group. But it only works if the attacker believes the allies will really turn up.

apply.text: That is why the question Zelensky describes is so big. Ukraine would give up Donbas, contested since 2014, in return for NATO's shield. Zelensky wants Article 5-style guarantees as a minimum. But Washington reportedly rules out US troops in Ukraine, and Russia calls Ukrainian NATO membership a red line.

practice.q: Same small country and alliance, but four of the nine allies say they will not send troops. What does the attacker face now?
practice.answer: Allies still helping: 9 − 4 = 5. Their strength: 5 × 30 = 150 units. Add the country's own 20: 150 + 20 = 170 units. 170 ÷ 100 = 1.7 times the attacker. Still stronger, but far less than 2.9. Every ally that stays out weakens the promise.

stories.headline: Hotter US prices raise Fed hike odds, adding pressure on RBI
stories.question: If the US Fed raises rates again, why could your EMI in India rise?
stories.dek: US prices rose faster than expected in October, so a December Fed hike looks likely. Higher US rates can pull money out of India, weaken the rupee and push the RBI to hike too.

so_far.text: An energy price shock from the Iran war has pushed inflation back up. On 16 September the US Federal Reserve (the Fed) raised its main rate to 3.75–4%. It was its first rise since July 2023. In November the Bank of England raised its rate to 4%, its first rise since August 2023. In India, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) raised its repo rate to 5.50% in 2026. On 7 October the rupee was near 96.58 per dollar.

what_happened.text: Market summaries say US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October from September, above the 0.3% forecast. Core prices, which leave out food and energy, rose 0.3%, a third straight month at that pace. Traders then priced about 88.7% odds of a quarter-point Fed hike in December, and 11.3% odds of a half-point. Bloomberg's 14 November roundup said the report supports a hike. On 14 November Bank of England chief economist Huw Pill said more rises will likely be needed in 2027. Markets still price two more European Central Bank (ECB) hikes.

steps.text: October's US prices beat forecasts, so inflation is not cooling and the Fed is expected to hike again.
Higher US rates make dollar bonds pay more, so global funds have less reason to hold Indian assets.
When funds sell Indian assets and buy dollars, the rupee weakens; it was near 96.58 per dollar on 7 October.
A weaker rupee makes imported oil and goods dearer, adding to Indian inflation that DBS sees above the RBI's target range.
That pushes the RBI toward another hike, which DBS expects in December, making loans costlier.

history.text:
The root of this story is inflation that would not go away. US prices have stayed above the Fed's 2% target for nearly six years. Central banks raised rates, then stopped in 2023. The RBI's last hike before 2026 came in February 2023. The Fed's came in July 2023, and the Bank of England's in August 2023. For a while, the Fed expected its next move to be a cut.

In 2026 the Fed held its rate at 3.5–3.75% for its first five meetings, though it had earlier expected to cut. Then the Iran war drove energy prices up, and inflation picked up again. US inflation slowed to 3.5% in June, but stayed well above target. On 20 July the Houthis announced a maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia. Brent crude, a world oil benchmark, passed $100 a barrel, and US petrol topped $4 a gallon. In July three Fed officials voted for a hike.

That flipped the direction. On 16 September the Fed raised its rate to 3.75–4%, 12 votes to 0, in Kevin Warsh's first move as chair. In 2026 the RBI also raised its repo rate to 5.50%, its first hike since February 2023. By 7 October the rupee was near 96.58 per dollar as money left Indian shares. In November the Bank of England raised its rate to 4%, its first rise since August 2023.

lesson.concept: How a Fed hike pulls money out of India
lesson.big_idea: Global money goes where it earns the most, after counting currency moves. When US rates rise, India's extra return shrinks, money leaves, the rupee weakens, and the RBI may hike to respond.

steps.title: Money chases the best return
steps.text: Big global funds compare what bonds pay in different countries. A bond is a loan to a government or company that pays a yearly return, called its yield.

steps.title: The currency counts too
steps.text: A foreign fund buys rupees to invest in India and sells them at the end. If the rupee falls meanwhile, it gets fewer dollars back and loses part of its return.

steps.title: A Fed hike shrinks India's edge
steps.text: When the Fed raises its rate, now 3.75–4%, US bonds tend to pay more. India's extra return shrinks, so some funds sell Indian assets and move into dollars.

steps.title: Outflows weaken the rupee
steps.text: Selling rupees for dollars pushes the rupee down. On 7 October it was near 96.58 per dollar, on a firm dollar, higher global yields and equity outflows. Imported oil then costs more.

steps.title: The RBI can answer with a hike
steps.text: Raising the repo rate, now 5.50%, lifts Indian yields and wins back some edge. The cost is dearer loans at home. DBS expects another RBI hike in December.

example.setup: Say a global fund can buy a US government bond paying 4% a year, or an Indian one paying 7%. Assume it expects the rupee to fall 2% a year against the dollar.

lines.label: India's extra return
lines.note: What India pays above the US.

lines.label: Minus the rupee's fall
lines.note: The fund loses 2% when converting back to dollars.

lines.label: Fed hikes: US pays 5%
lines.note: India's edge is gone, so money may leave.

lines.label: RBI hikes: India pays 7.5%
lines.note: Some edge returns, but loans in India cost more.

example.result: A one-point rise in US returns wiped out India's edge. Money tends to leave, which weakens the rupee. An RBI hike can win back some edge, at the cost of dearer loans at home.

apply.text: US prices rose 0.4% in October against a 0.3% forecast, and traders put 88.7% odds on a December quarter-point Fed hike. Like the US bond in our example, that would lift US returns and shrink India's edge again. The rupee was already near 96.58 per dollar on 7 October. DBS expects a second RBI hike in December.

practice.q: Same fund, US bond at 5% and Indian bond at 7.5%, but now it expects the rupee to fall 3% a year. Does India still have an edge?
practice.answer: Start with India's extra return: 7.5% − 5% = 2.5 points. Subtract the rupee's expected fall: 2.5 − 3 = −0.5 point. The edge is negative, so the fund earns more in the US. A falling rupee can undo an RBI hike.

so_far.text: India and the US began talks on a bilateral trade agreement, a two-country deal on tariffs, in March 2025. In August 2025 the US raised its tariff on Indian goods to 50%. On 7 February 2026 the two sides released an interim framework that cut the tariff to 18%. On 22 June 2026 Goyal said signing was taking longer because of the 50% tariff. He also said India was aiming for preferential access.

what_happened.text: In remarks reported on 15 November 2026, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said India and the US have agreed on preferential market access for Indian goods in America. Under the proposed bilateral trade agreement, he said, Indian goods will face lower US tariffs than goods from competing countries. The Hindu, Mint, Deccan Herald and other newspapers reported his remarks. The deal was meant to be signed earlier, but changes in the US tariff landscape led to further negotiations. No signing date, list of goods or size of the tariff gap has been reported.

steps.text: A tariff is a tax US importers pay on foreign goods, so it raises what American buyers pay.
US buyers can often choose similar goods from several countries, so they compare the final price after the tariff.
If Indian goods face a lower tariff than rivals' goods, Goyal's promise means they reach US buyers cheaper.
Cheaper prices can shift US orders away from rival countries' exporters and towards Indian exporters.
How much India gains depends on the size of the tariff gap and the goods covered; neither has been reported.

history.text: The story starts in March 2025, when India and the US began talks on a bilateral trade agreement. By mid-2025 they had finished five rounds and hoped to agree a first stage by October–November 2025. Then the talks stalled. On 7 August 2025 the US put a 25% reciprocal tariff on Indian goods. On 27 August it added another 25% as a penalty for India buying Russian oil. That made 50%, and a sixth round of talks was postponed. The turning point came on 7 February 2026. The two sides released an interim framework, a first outline of the deal. The US tariff fell from 50% to 18%, and the oil penalty was removed. In return India committed to stop importing Russian oil, directly or indirectly. The US said it may reconsider the relief if imports resume. The framework named sectors expected to benefit: chemicals, gems and jewellery, textiles, engineering goods, auto components, pharmaceuticals and electronics. Reports also cite $500bn of US purchases over five years; Outlook India reported that this goal is not binding. On 22 June 2026 Goyal said signing was taking longer because of the 50% tariff, and that India wanted preferential access. Changes in the US tariff landscape then forced more negotiations. On 15 November 2026 Goyal said that preferential access has been agreed.

lesson.concept: How a tariff edge over rival countries works
lesson.big_idea: A tariff is a tax on imports, added to the price at the border. If India's goods are taxed less than a rival's, they reach American buyers cheaper, which can win orders.

steps.title: A tariff is a border tax
steps.text: When a US company imports goods, it pays a tariff, a percentage of the goods' value, to the US government. Under the February 2026 framework, that rate for Indian goods is 18%.

steps.title: The tax lifts the landed price
steps.text: The landed price is the goods' value plus the tariff. Importers usually pass much of this cost on, so it shapes what shops and buyers in the US pay.

steps.title: Buyers compare countries
steps.text: A US buyer can often get similar goods from several countries. They compare the landed price from each and tend to pick the cheapest that meets their needs.

steps.title: The gap is the edge
steps.text: Preferential access means a lower tariff than rivals pay. What matters is the gap between India's rate and the rival's rate, not India's rate alone. Goyal says India will get this.

steps.title: Cheaper price or bigger margin
steps.text: An exporter can use the edge in two ways: charge less and win more orders, or keep the same price and earn more on each sale.

example.setup: Imagine an Indian garment maker and a rival factory abroad. Both sell an identical shirt to a US store for $10. India's tariff is 18%; assume the rival's is 20%.

example.result: A two-point tariff gap makes the Indian shirt 20 cents cheaper. That is small per item, but across big orders it can decide who wins the contract. A bigger gap means a bigger edge.

apply.text: So when Goyal says Indian goods will face lower US tariffs than competing countries, he is describing this gap. The February framework already cut India's own rate from 50% to 18%. The new promise is about how India's rate compares with rivals'. Until the gap and the goods are published, nobody can work out the real edge.

practice.q: Same store, but now the shirt is worth $20. India's tariff is 18%; assume the rival's is 25%. How big is India's edge per shirt?
practice.answer: India: 18% of $20 = $3.60, so the landed price is $23.60. Rival: 25% of $20 = $5, so the landed price is $25. Edge: $25 − $23.60 = $1.40 per shirt.

scenes.say: Phir mamla bigad gaya. 7 August 2025 ko US ne Indian goods pe 25 percent tariff laga diya. 27 August ko Russian oil kharidne ki penalty ke taur pe 25 percent aur jod diya. Kul hua 50 percent, aur agle round ki baatcheet tal gayi.
scenes.speak: फिर मामला बिगड़ गया। 7 August 2025 को US ने Indian goods पे 25 percent tariff लगा दिया। 27 August को Russian oil खरीदने की penalty के तौर पे 25 percent और जोड़ दिया। कुल हुआ 50 percent, और अगले round की बातचीत टल गई।

scenes.speak: अब वो एक idea जो सीखना है: tariff edge काम कैसे करता है। Tariff imports पे tax है, जो border पे price में जुड़ जाता है। अगर India के goods पे rival से कम tax लगता है, तो वो American buyers तक सस्ते पहुँचते हैं। और इससे orders मिल सकते हैं।

scenes.speak: अब मान लो rival पे tariff 20 percent है। वो हुआ 2 dollar, तो उसकी shirt 12 dollar में land होती है। India का edge है 20 cent per shirt। 10 हज़ार shirts पे, यह हुआ 2 हज़ार dollar। Gap जितना बड़ा, edge उतना बड़ा।

Nayi preferential access mein yeh cover hain ya nahi, ab tak pata nahi hai. Agar aap export business mein kaam karte hain, toh tariff edge ka matlab ho sakta hai zyada US orders. Zyadatar gharon ke liye, prices pe ab tak koi seedha asar nahi hai.

scenes.say: Ek aam galti: Goyal ke bayan ka matlab yeh nahi ki deal sign ho gayi. Yeh ab bhi ek proposed agreement hai. Aur hamare lesson se yaad rakhiye, asli edge India ke rate aur rivals ke rates ke gap pe depend karta hai. February framework India ka apna rate pehle hi ghata chuka hai. Jab tak gap publish nahi hota, koi nahi bata sakta ki India ko asal mein milta kya hai.

scenes.say: Aage kya dekhna hai? Signing date. Un goods ki list jinhe kam tariff milega, aur kya February wale sectors usmein hain. Competing countries ke mukable tariff gap ka size. Aur US ke tariff landscape mein exactly kya badla. Inmein se kisi ki bhi date announce nahi hui hai.

stories.headline: Indian families' share of health bills falls to 42.7%
stories.question: Indians now pay less of their own medical bills, but is healthcare actually cheaper?
stories.dek: Households paid 42.7% of India's health spending in 2023-24, down from 64.2% a decade earlier. That shows others, like government and insurers, now pay more. It does not show care got cheaper.

so_far.text: India tracks who pays for health care through the National Health Accounts, official estimates of health spending. In 2013-14, households paid 64.2% of all health spending directly. In 2017, the National Health Policy set a target: public health spending of 2.5% of GDP by 2025. The household share fell to a low of 39.4% in 2021-22. Then it rose to 43.4% in 2022-23, in accounts released in May 2026. Those accounts put government spending at 1.48% of GDP.

what_happened.text: On 15 November 2026, the National Health Accounts for 2023-24 were released, the 11th round of these estimates. Households paid 42.7% of all health spending out of their own pockets, down from 64.2% in 2013-14. That is a fall of 21.5 percentage points. But in 2022-23 the figure was 43.4%, so the latest yearly fall is under one point. Government health spending reached ₹4.14 lakh crore, more than three times the ₹1.30 lakh crore of 2013-14. About ₹1.53 lakh crore went to primary care. Private insurance's share rose to 10.2%, from 3.4%, and social security's to 11%, from 6%.

steps.text: The out-of-pocket share is what households pay directly, divided by all health spending in India.
Government health spending more than tripled in ten years, from ₹1.30 lakh crore to ₹4.14 lakh crore.
Private insurance rose from 3.4% to 10.2% of spending, and social security from 6% to 11%.
When others pay more, the total bill grows, so the households' slice shrinks even if their rupees don't.
So the share shows who pays, not whether treatment itself has become cheaper.

history.text:
The story starts in 2013-14. That year, Indian households paid 64.2% of all health spending directly, at the hospital or chemist. The government spent ₹1.30 lakh crore, about 1.15% of GDP, the value of everything India produces in a year.

In 2017, the National Health Policy set a target: public health spending of 2.5% of GDP by 2025. This gave the country a yardstick for public money in health.

The household share then fell sharply. By 2021-22 it reached a low of 39.4%, and the government paid 48% of all health spending.

How much the government really spends stayed disputed. In April 2024, a Lancet-linked report put government health spending near 1.2% of GDP. The government disputed it, saying spending was at a record high.

The 2025 deadline passed with the 2.5% target unmet. The Centre's own share, separate from the states, was only about 0.29% of GDP in 2025-26, against an aim of 1%.

In May 2026, the 2022-23 accounts put government spending at 1.48% of GDP on a revised GDP series. The household share was back up at 43.4%. The 2023-24 accounts, released on 15 November 2026, show 42.7%: far below 2013-14, but above the 2021-22 low.

analogy.text: Picture a group dinner. Ten years ago you paid nearly two-thirds of the bill. Now friends chip in more, and you pay well under half. Your slice shrank. But if the group ordered more, or prices rose, your own rupees could still be higher.
analogy.breaks: In health care, the 'friends' are government and insurers, and households partly fund them through taxes and insurance premiums.

for_you.text: When your family pays a hospital, clinic or chemist directly, that is out-of-pocket spending. In 2023-24, 42.7 of every 100 rupees spent on health in India still came this way. More now comes from government and insurers; private insurance pays 10.2%. But these figures do not show whether your own bills fell, so they cannot tell you care got cheaper.

lesson.concept: How a share can fall while the bill grows
lesson.big_idea: The out-of-pocket share is what families pay directly, divided by the whole health bill. It can fall because others pay more, even while families pay the same or more rupees.

steps.title: Count the whole health bill
steps.text: Total health spending is everything spent on care in a country in a year: by government, by insurers, by social security schemes and by families themselves. Think of it as one big bill.

steps.title: Out-of-pocket is paid directly
steps.text: Out-of-pocket spending is money families pay at the hospital, clinic or chemist that nobody pays back. In India it was 42.7% of all health spending in 2023-24, down from 64.2% in 2013-14.

steps.title: Share is part divided by whole
steps.text: The out-of-pocket share is family payments divided by the whole bill, times 100. If government and insurers add money, the whole bill grows. India's government health spending more than tripled, and private insurance's share rose from 3.4% to 10.2%.

steps.title: A share is not a price
steps.text: A smaller share tells you who pays, not how much care costs. To know whether families spend fewer rupees, you need the rupee total for households, not just their share.

example.setup: Imagine a town spends ₹100 crore on health in a year, and families pay ₹60 crore of it directly. Ten years later families pay ₹70 crore, and the town's total bill is ₹175 crore.

lines.label: Share then
lines.note: Families pay 60 of every 100 rupees.

lines.label: Families pay later
lines.note: Families spend ₹10 crore more than before.

lines.label: Others pay later
lines.note: Government and insurers, up from ₹40 crore.

lines.label: Share now
lines.note: Family payments over the bigger total.

lines.label: Change in share
lines.note: The share fell sharply, yet family rupees rose.

example.result: The families' share fell by 20 points while they paid ₹10 crore more. A falling share shows others paying more; it cannot by itself show care got cheaper.

apply.text: India's household share fell from 64.2% to 42.7%, while government health spending rose from ₹1.30 lakh crore to ₹4.14 lakh crore and private insurance's share tripled. That is our town's pattern: others grew the bill. Whether families paid fewer rupees needs the household rupee total, which the reported figures do not give.

practice.q: Same town, but later families pay ₹45 crore and the total health bill is ₹150 crore. What is the share, and did families pay less?
practice.answer: Share = ₹45 crore ÷ ₹150 crore = 0.3, or 30%. Families paid ₹45 crore, down from ₹60 crore, so ₹15 crore less. Here the share fell and family rupees fell too. You only know that because you have the rupee totals.

takeaways: A share can fall while the bill grows, if others pay a bigger part.
Households paid 42.7% of health spending in 2023-24, down from 64.2%; that alone doesn't prove care is cheaper.
Watch for total health spending figures and progress toward the unmet 2.5%-of-GDP target.

stories.headline: Cyclone Akvan heads for Andhra coast; Odisha and Bengal brace for rain
stories.question: Where will Cyclone Akvan hit, and how bad will it be for Odisha and Bengal?
stories.dek: IMD expects the storm to move north-northwest toward Andhra Pradesh but has not named a landfall point. Odisha may see heavy rain and 40–50 kmph gusts, and Bengal's coast faces rain.

so_far.text: On 14 November 2026, the India Meteorological Department (IMD), India's weather agency, reported a well-marked low over the southeast Bay of Bengal. A well-marked low is a patch of low air pressure where winds start to circle. IMD said it would become a depression within 24 hours and a cyclonic storm by the evening of 16 November. At the severe stage, IMD expected winds of 85–95 kmph, gusting to 105 kmph. It named no landfall point.

what_happened.text: By 15 November 2026 the low had become a depression. It was about 1,010 km south-southeast of Visakhapatnam and 1,130 km south-southeast of Gopalpur in Odisha. IMD expects it to become Cyclonic Storm Akvan by 16 November, a severe cyclonic storm by 17 November, and possibly a very severe cyclonic storm by 19 November. It is moving north-northwest toward the Andhra Pradesh coast. IMD has not named a landfall point. Fishermen are told not to go to sea from 18 to 21 November.

steps.text: A cyclone draws its energy from warm sea water, so it keeps strengthening while it stays over the open Bay.
Akvan was still about 1,010 km out at sea on 15 November, giving it days to grow.
Its track points north-northwest, toward the Andhra Pradesh coast, rather than straight at Odisha or Bengal.
Odisha may see gusts of 40–50 kmph on 18 November, far below the storm's projected peak gusts of 145 kmph.
Rain bands spread much wider, so Puri, Ganjam, Gajapati and coastal Bengal districts still face heavy rain.

history.text:
Akvan's history is the storm's own short life. It began on 14 November 2026, when IMD reported a well-marked low over the southeast Bay of Bengal. IMD forecast a depression within 24 hours and a cyclone by the evening of 16 November. That gave coastal states about two days' notice. IMD expected severe-stage winds of 85–95 kmph, gusting to 105 kmph, but named no landfall point. Hindustan Times reported that Odisha was on heavy rain alert.

On 15 November the forecast held, and the low became a depression. The New Indian Express reported that Odisha was waiting for heavy rains. IMD's outlook then grew. It now sees a possible very severe cyclonic storm by 19 November, with gusts of 145 kmph. That is 40 kmph above the earlier severe-stage gust figure. IMD also gave a direction: north-northwest toward Andhra Pradesh. It still gave no landfall point.

lesson.concept: Why stronger wind does far more damage
lesson.big_idea: The push of wind grows with the square of its speed. If the wind is twice as fast, it pushes on a roof or tree four times harder, not two.

steps.title: Wind is moving air
steps.text: Wind is air in motion. When it hits a wall, a roof or a tree, it pushes. Faster air carries more energy, so it pushes harder.

steps.title: Push grows with speed squared
steps.text: The push rises with speed multiplied by itself. This is called 'squared'. Twice the speed gives two times two, so four times the push. Three times the speed gives nine times the push.

steps.title: Sustained winds and gusts
steps.text: A sustained wind is the steady average speed. A gust is a short burst above it. Gusts often break things because the push jumps suddenly. For Akvan, IMD projects gusts up to 145 kmph.

steps.title: Strongest near the centre
steps.text: A cyclone's fiercest winds circle close to its centre. Further away, winds are much weaker. Rain bands, though, can stretch far from the centre.

steps.title: The ladder of storm stages
steps.text: IMD names stages as wind rises: depression, cyclonic storm, severe, then very severe. For Akvan it projects 85–95 kmph at severe and 120–130 kmph at very severe.

example.setup: Imagine a tin roof that feels 1 unit of push from a 50 kmph wind. What happens when the wind rises to 100 kmph, then 150 kmph?

lines.label: Speed ratio at 100
lines.note: The wind is twice as fast.

lines.label: Push at 100 kmph
lines.note: Square the ratio; don't just double it.

lines.label: Speed ratio at 150
lines.note: The wind is three times as fast.

lines.label: Push at 150 kmph
lines.note: Nine times the push of a 50 kmph wind.

example.result: Tripling the wind speed multiplies the push by nine. So each step up the storm ladder is far more dangerous than the speed numbers alone suggest.

apply.text: Akvan's very severe gusts are projected at 145 kmph. Odisha may see gusts of 40–50 kmph on 18 November. 145 ÷ 50 is about 2.9, and 2.9 × 2.9 is about 8.4. So the storm's peak gusts could push roughly eight times harder than the gusts Odisha may see. Odisha's main forecast is heavy rain on 19 November.

practice.q: At the severe stage, IMD expects gusts of 105 kmph. How much harder does that gust push than a 35 kmph breeze?
practice.answer: First find the speed ratio: 105 ÷ 35 = 3. Then square it: 3 × 3 = 9. The 105 kmph gust pushes nine times harder than the 35 kmph breeze.

stories.headline: US Treasury tells Nvidia to hire an outside chief executive
stories.question: Why is the US Treasury telling Nvidia to bring in an outside CEO?
stories.dek: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wants a 'dramatic shake-up' and answers on whether Nvidia pushed 'seemingly illicit' chip sales to China. It is the latest turn in a Washington fight over AI chips and China.

so_far.text: Megaspeed is an Nvidia customer. On CNBC on 13 November, Bessent said Treasury, State, Defense and the US trade office (USTR) had favoured putting it on the Entity List, a US trade blacklist, 'for months'. Commerce has not listed it. On 11 November Axios reported that Bessent confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over this. CNN reported that Trump's advisers have discussed a possible Lutnick ouster. NPR reported that Commerce is under pressure for delaying export controls on Nvidia chips. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO on 12 November.

what_happened.text: On 15 November Bloomberg reported that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged Nvidia to hire a chief executive from outside the company. He wants answers within 10 days on whether Nvidia pushed 'seemingly illicit' chip sales to China to boost revenue. Bessent said Nvidia needed a 'dramatic shake-up' after Huang's exit. Colette Kress, Nvidia's finance chief, is interim CEO. Bloomberg says Nvidia faces intense pressure as it searches for a new leader. Semafor reported that Lutnick is expected to fly with President Trump to China.

steps.text: The US bars its top AI chips, such as Nvidia's Blackwell, from being sold to China.
In general, selling US chips to an Entity List firm needs a licence; an unlisted buyer faces fewer checks.
Four departments wanted Megaspeed listed for months; Commerce did not act, so Bessent blames Lutnick.
Treasury now asks whether Nvidia itself pushed 'seemingly illicit' China sales to boost revenue.
So Bessent wants a 'dramatic shake-up', led by a CEO from outside Nvidia.

history.text: The story starts with a 2025 bargain. In August 2025 the US agreed to take 15% of Nvidia and AMD chip sales to China in return for export licences, and Bessent defended the deal. This changed China sales from a grey area into something allowed, but taxed. In November 2025 the White House drew a firmer line. It said it did not plan to let Nvidia sell its top chip, Blackwell, to China. So the best chips were meant to stay out. A money worry grew alongside. In January 2026 Senate Democrats asked FSOC, a council of US financial regulators, to study the risks of AI debt. A summary of the Fed's May 2026 report says it listed AI valuations and debt-funded spending among the risks market contacts raised most. For months, Bessent says, Treasury, State, Defense and USTR wanted Megaspeed blacklisted, but Commerce held off. In November 2026 it broke open. Axios reported the Bessent–Lutnick clash on 11 November. Huang resigned on 12 November. On 13 November the Fed said AI and data-centre debt topped $680 billion in ten months. On 15 November Bessent turned his pressure on Nvidia itself.

lesson.concept: How US export controls decide who gets AI chips
lesson.big_idea: The US government decides which buyers abroad may get its advanced chips. Commerce keeps a blacklist called the Entity List, and any risky buyer left off it can become a gap.

steps.title: Some exports need permission
steps.text: An export licence is government permission to sell certain goods abroad. For advanced AI chips, the US checks who is buying and where the chips will end up before it says yes.

steps.title: The Entity List is a blacklist
steps.text: The Commerce Department keeps the Entity List, a list of foreign firms seen as risks. Selling American chips to a listed firm needs a licence, which is usually refused. Treasury, State, Defense and USTR wanted Megaspeed on it.

steps.title: Licences can carry conditions
steps.text: Permission can come with strings. In August 2025 the US agreed to take 15% of Nvidia and AMD chip sales to China in return for licences. The top Blackwell chip was not meant for China at all.

steps.title: Middlemen are the weak spot

apply.text: Bessent says Treasury, State, Defense and USTR wanted Megaspeed on the Entity List for months, but Commerce, which keeps the list, did not act. Now he is asking Nvidia directly whether it pushed 'seemingly illicit' China sales to boost revenue, and wants a CEO from outside to lead a 'dramatic shake-up'.

practice.q: Suppose ChipCo makes a licensed $200 million sale of its older chip to China under the same 15% deal. How much does the government take, and how much does ChipCo keep?
practice.answer: Step 1: the government's cut is 15% of $200 million = $30 million. Step 2: ChipCo keeps $200 million − $30 million = $170 million.

stories.headline: Why Microsoft's Outlook and Teams outage lasted more than a day
stories.question: What caused Microsoft's outage that shut down Outlook and Teams for over a day?
stories.dek: Many email servers failed health checks and the rest buckled under the load. A network change coincided with the start. Microsoft says it was no cyberattack, but the final cause is unconfirmed.

so_far.text: Microsoft 365 is Microsoft's set of online work tools. Outlook email for businesses runs on a cloud service called Exchange Online. The set also includes Teams, SharePoint Online, the Copilot assistant and the Defender XDR security tool. These services run in Microsoft's data centres, not on your own computer. So one fault can reach users in many countries at once. Big cloud outages have happened before: Microsoft had them in January 2023 and October 2025, and Amazon's cloud failed for nearly 15 hours in October 2025.

what_happened.text: The disruption began on Thursday 12 November 2026. Microsoft first said users in the Americas could not reach their Exchange Online mailboxes. It later listed Teams, SharePoint Online, Copilot and Defender XDR as possibly affected. Downdetector showed users hit in more than 70 countries and territories. Singapore's government email went down, the Philippine Supreme Court's email was affected, and Japan's government IT was hit. In the US, Detroit's city offices were affected. Early on Saturday 14 November, Microsoft said it had restored service to all remaining customers and regions, after more than 24 hours. Microsoft said the cause was a technical issue, not a cyberattack.

steps.text: Exchange Online runs on many servers, and automated health checks keep testing each one to see if it works.
From 12 November, many of those servers failed their health checks and became unavailable.
The same users landed on fewer servers, so processors ran hot and the secure-connection process was overwhelmed.
Traffic had not risen, so the trouble was lost capacity, not a sudden rush of users.
A network configuration change coincided with the start; Microsoft began rolling it back but had not confirmed the final root cause.

history.text:
Many offices now keep their email, chat and files on a few giant cloud services. That is convenient, but it also means one fault can spread a long way.

In January 2023 a Microsoft 365 outage hit Teams and Outlook, including users in India. Microsoft blamed a change to its wide area network, the network linking its sites, and rolled the change back.

On 19 July 2024 the risk became much bigger. A faulty CrowdStrike update crashed about 8.5 million Windows systems. It was called the largest IT outage in history. It cancelled 5,078 flights in one day, and the firm Parametrix estimated top US companies lost nearly $5.4 billion. It was not a cyberattack. The cancelled flights showed that one bad update can disrupt the physical world, not just screens.

In October 2025 came two more warnings. On 19–20 October, Amazon's AWS cloud failed in its us-east-1 region for nearly 15 hours. Firms with no AWS contract were hit too, through vendors that depended on it. On 29 October, a problem in Microsoft's Azure Front Door disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot and Xbox Live for hours. Microsoft fixed it by going back to a last known good configuration.

So by November 2026, several outages had shown how one fault at one provider could disrupt work in many places at once.

lesson.concept: How one server failure cascades into an outage
lesson.big_idea: Big online services share users across many servers. If some drop out, the same work lands on fewer machines. They overload, look broken, and get removed too, so a partial fault snowballs.

steps.title: Work is shared across servers
steps.text: A service like Outlook email runs on many servers. A load balancer, a kind of traffic director, spreads users across them so no single machine carries too much.

steps.title: Health checks remove sick servers
steps.text: Automated health checks test each server regularly. A server that fails is pulled out, so users are not sent to it. Microsoft said many Exchange Online servers failed these checks.

steps.title: The load moves to survivors
steps.text: Users do not vanish. Their work shifts to the servers still running, so each carries more and processor use climbs. Microsoft saw this on remaining servers, though traffic had not risen.

steps.title: Overload spreads the failure
steps.text: An overloaded server answers slowly, so it can fail its own health check and be pulled too. Users who retry open new secure connections, which cost extra processing. The loop feeds itself.

steps.title: Recovery must be gradual
steps.text: Undoing the trigger is not enough. If servers return all at once, the waiting crowd can knock them over again. Microsoft began rolling back a network change; Lamanna said recovery was harder than normal.

example.setup: Imagine an email service running on 10 servers. Assume each can safely handle 100 users at once. On a normal morning, 600 users are online.

lines.label: Normal load
lines.note: Well under the 100 limit.

lines.label: Half fail checks
lines.note: Assume a bad change knocks out five.

lines.label: New load
lines.note: Same users, fewer servers: 20 over the limit.

lines.label: Two more drop
lines.note: Overloaded servers fail their own health checks.

lines.label: The spiral
lines.note: Double the safe limit, with zero new users.

example.result: Traffic never rose, yet losing half the servers pushed the rest past their limit, and the overload removed even more. That is how a partial fault becomes a full outage.

apply.text: Microsoft described this pattern: many Exchange Online servers failed health checks, the rest ran hot with an overwhelmed secure-connection process, and traffic had not risen. A network configuration change coincided with the start, and Microsoft began rolling it back, but the final cause is unconfirmed. Full service returned only early on 14 November.

practice.q: Same service: 10 servers, each safe up to 100 users, 600 users online. If only 3 servers fail, are the rest overloaded?
practice.answer: Servers left: 10 − 3 = 7. Load: 600 ÷ 7 ≈ 86 users each. That is under the 100 limit, so the service slows a little but holds. The cascade starts only when load per server crosses the limit, which here happens once 5 or more servers fail.

scenes.speak: अब वो एक idea जो सीखना है: एक failure cascade कैसे बनता है। बड़े services users को बहुत सारे servers में बाँट देते हैं, एक traffic director के ज़रिए जिसे load balancer कहते हैं। और health checks हर उस server को बाहर कर देते हैं जो खराब लगता है।

scenes.say: Lekin users gayab nahi hote. Unka kaam bache hue servers par chala jaata hai. Woh overload hote hain, dheere jawab dete hain, apne health checks mein fail hote hain, aur woh bhi bahar ho jaate hain. Jo users retry karte hain, woh naye secure connections kholte hain, jinmein extra processing lagti hai. Socho ek toll plaza jahan aadhe booth band ho jaayein: gaadiyan utni hi, lanes kam, aur jam badhta jaata hai.
scenes.speak: लेकिन users गायब नहीं होते। उनका काम बचे हुए servers पर चला जाता है। वो overload होते हैं, धीरे जवाब देते हैं, अपने health checks में fail होते हैं, और वो भी बाहर हो जाते हैं। जो users retry करते हैं, वो नए secure connections खोलते हैं, जिनमें extra processing लगती है। सोचो एक toll plaza जहाँ आधे booth बंद हो जाएँ: गाड़ियाँ उतनी ही, lanes कम, और jam बढ़ता जाता है।

scenes.say: Isiliye recovery dheere dheere karni padti hai. Trigger ko undo karna kaafi nahi hai. Saare servers ek saath wapas laaye, toh intezaar kar rahi bheed unhe phir se gira sakti hai.
scenes.speak: इसीलिए recovery धीरे धीरे करनी पड़ती है। Trigger को undo करना काफ़ी नहीं है। सारे servers एक साथ वापस लाए, तो इंतज़ार कर रही भीड़ उन्हें फिर से गिरा सकती है।

Ek network change shuruaat ke waqt hi hua tha, aur Microsoft ne use rollback karna shuru kiya.
scenes.show: Myth: a hack. Fact: technical fault
scenes.speak: एक आम myth है कि यह hack था। Microsoft कहता है कि यह technical issue था, कोई malicious activity नहीं। और Microsoft ने जो बताया, वो हमारे example से match करता है: कई servers health checks में fail, बाकी overload, और traffic flat। एक network change शुरुआत के वक़्त ही हुआ था, और Microsoft ने उसे rollback करना शुरू किया।

scenes.say: Aage kya dekhna hai? Microsoft ne ek post incident report ka vaada kiya hai, jismein final root cause ka naam hona chahiye. scenes.speak: आगे क्या देखना है? Microsoft ने एक post incident report का वादा किया है, जिसमें final root cause का नाम होना चाहिए। यह report हमारे sources में available नहीं थी, और कोई date तय नहीं है। यह भी पता नहीं कि customers को service credits मिलेंगे या नहीं, और कोई regulator जाँच करेगा या नहीं।
